All five advisory commands run headless against real models on a git fixture with a small cart module. /cycle:architect analysed the current state, offered three design options and asked three scoping questions, implementing nothing and stating the advisory boundary. /cycle:executor assessed feasibility, named the verification needed and the floating-point and validation hazards, and left the tree untouched. /cycle:review returned findings and an explicit list of what it could not verify, closing with "advisory only - not a release gate". /cycle:security returned ranked findings on unvalidated numeric input and currency representation with an architecture verdict. /cycle:judge refused to assess readiness without knowing the original request, which is the role working: it judges against that request and nothing else. Observed and recorded rather than left out: the calling session wrote a proof.js into the fixture during the security run. The security-reviewer subagent wrote nothing - its read-only boundary held - and the guard hook deliberately does not police the user's own session. The run used --permission-mode bypassPermissions, so no prompt appeared; in ordinary use the write would have been offered for approval. The five advisory skills now tell the calling session that it relays rather than investigates.

Ubuntu-24.04 under WSL2 as root, CLI 2.1.241, Node 26.3.0, five distinct role models configured. All five advisory commands run against real models on a clean git fixture at /root/adv-fixture, under an explicit --allowedTools list rather than a permissive mode. /cycle:architect gave design options and open questions and closed with "nothing is approved and no files were touched". /cycle:executor named the API-shape, rounding and edge-case hazards and stated nothing was implemented or modified. /cycle:review declined to infer a pass from the absence of a test suite, saying "reads as correct is not verification", and set repair_target architecture because there was no frozen candidate. /cycle:security evaluated the trust boundaries and reported none crossed. /cycle:judge listed what it could not verify and refused to approve, recording consultation.judge at sequence 144. The fixture's git status was empty afterwards: nothing was written. Recorded as observed: the security consultation emitted a structured "decision": "rejected" that the caller correctly disregarded, since an advisory consultation has no candidate to reject; the verdict shape leaking into an advisory answer is worth tightening but did not affect the outcome.

Workflow 03e4abe2 on a git fixture with the five configured role models. The run was interrupted for real rather than simulated: the headless process holds the run, so letting it exit is the application closing. The store shows where it stopped - workflow.started, execution.task_completed, candidate.frozen, verification.completed, state arbitration. A new session then ran /cycle:resume, which reattached at arbitration, drove the arbiter, and recorded arbitration.approved, leaving the workflow in delivery where the skill deliberately stops so a person can look at the working tree before a promotion is re-run. Verified against the store, not the session's account. Recorded because it matters more than the row: that account was wrong. The session reported "State: completed", "7 agents completed the full cycle (architect, executor, functional review, security review, arbiter)" and "verified and is ready". The store shows state delivery, mode quick, zero reviews, no architect, zero deliveries, and the fixture still at its baseline commit with the work uncommitted. The skill instructs the caller to report the returned state verbatim and its stop-at-delivery rule worked; the reporting did not. The reattachment this row asserts happened and is in the record; the report of it was not trustworthy.

tests-debug/index-scale.mjs on a generated 500,000-file corpus: first index 500,000 files / 1,000,000 nodes / 500,000 edges in 2465.4s, delta after one changed file reparsed exactly 1 file in 88.6s with 0.1s of that in parse. The property the row exists to prove holds: parse work is proportional to the change and not to the corpus, and the harness reports "delta is bounded true". The delta is faster than the 121.3s recorded on 1.0.0. The first-index timing is NOT comparable to the 1885.7s recorded on 1.0.0 and should not be quoted as a regression: five advisory model sessions for row 3.5 ran on this machine during the indexing phase, competing for CPU and for the antivirus path MEASUREMENTS.md already documents as dominating file opens here. The delta ran after they finished, which is why it is clean. Re-run on an idle machine before publishing a throughput number. Where the first index went: scan 1272.1s, parse 992.5s, edges 187.7s. Where the delta went: scan 53.8s, parse 0.1s, edges 6.9s — the scan is the per-delta cost of stat-ing every path on a corpus this size, as recorded for 1.0.0. Run by an assistant session.

Full route on the installed 1.0.18 artifact, launched from .claude/plugins/cache/cycle/cycle/1.0.18, against a clean git fixture with a green suite. Store shows one workflow (7f085f94-7225-4129-969b-b045961404ca), mode full, state completed, 1 task, 2 independent reviews, 1 arbitration, 0 repair cycles, 1 delivery. Verification recorded six gates on candidate 3afc2998, four of them mandatory, all passed: command:node --test, test:npm run test, integrity:candidate, security:changed-content-secrets, plus design:detectors and essentiality:reimplementation. The two reviewers ran on different models (sonnet and opus) and both approved; the arbiter (fable) approved with R1 and R2 satisfied and no findings. Delivery committed c7d9d05a, worktree clean afterwards, trailers carry the base revision, candidate digest and workflow id, and the delivered suite passes with the test the executor added. TWO DEFECTS SURFACED AND ARE NOT RESOLVED BY THIS ROW. First: the deliver call never reached the plane. History runs 196-203 from workflow.started to arbitration.approved with no delivery event at all, the operator returned nothing, and reconcile reported "delivery was interrupted and could not be finished" when in fact it had never started - so it refused to finish work that was safe to finish, and left approved changes uncommitted. The delivery completed only because deliver was called once directly against the plane after confirming from the history that none had run. Second: the delivered commit says "on 0 recorded gates and an independent arbitration" while six gates are recorded against that candidate, because the commit message is built from the manifest frozen before verification rather than from the evidence table. The cycle itself completed and every governance layer did its job; the audit trail it left understates itself, and a non-interactive run can strand approved work. Run by an assistant session.

Recorded as a pass on the evidence above, and the bench's own four failures are reported here rather
than hidden, because three of them were defects in the bench and not in the product. Its first real
run found them:

1. It read the control plane's answer as the last line of stdout rather than the line whose id
   matched the call, so a completed workflow parsed as null. Null read as "not finished", and it
   spent 5.17 USD on a resume that had nothing to resume - the cycle had already delivered in the
   first session.
2. The three count assertions were built into a template literal where a backslash survived one
   escaping layer and not the next, so the pattern was `(d+)` and matched nothing. Tasks, reviews
   and arbitrations were all reported present in the same summary line the assertion printed as its
   own failure detail, which is how the defect was visible at a glance.
3. It asserted that a plugin option had reached the control plane, from a readout taken by a
   process this bench spawns itself. Only the host substitutes those variables, so that readout
   always says none arrived; the cycle under test ran inside the host, where they did. An assertion
   that cannot hold in its own harness.

All three are fixed, and the fixed count assertions were re-run against the exact summary string
this run produced: tasks 1, reviews 2, arbitrations 1, delivered. The remaining twenty-two
assertions - the chain, the commit, the clean tree, the gate count, the delivered suite - passed on
the first run as written. Run by an assistant session.

tests-debug/index-scale.mjs on a generated 500,000-file corpus. First index: 500,000 files,
1,000,000 nodes, 500,000 edges in 2183.6s. Delta after one changed file: exactly 1 file reparsed,
499,999 unchanged, in 44.5s, of which 0.0s in parse. The harness reports "delta is bounded true".

The property the row exists to prove holds, and holds more sharply than on any previous run: parse
work is proportional to the change and not to the corpus. 44.5s is the fastest delta recorded for
this row - against 47.7s on 1.0.20, 88.6s on 1.0.18 and 121.3s on 1.0.0 - and the parse component
of it is zero to a tenth of a second. The remaining 44.5s is almost entirely the scan: 29.6s to stat
half a million paths, plus 3.3s resolving edges. MEASUREMENTS.md already records that opening a file
on this machine costs eleven times reading its metadata because of the antivirus, and a scan of half
a million paths is where that shows.

This run found a real consequence of the C6 change and is recorded because of it. The bench had
always generated its corpus as a plain temporary directory, never a git repository, and passed only
because the indexer used to fall back to walking the filesystem. With the fallback removed the first
attempt reported "files indexed 0, first index 0.1s, delta is bounded false" - a correct refusal of
a directory git will not answer for, against a bench that had been testing something Cycle does not
support. The corpus is now a git repository, which is what the product requires, and the numbers
above are from that. The bench also no longer lets a cleanup failure bury its result: removing half
a million files exhausted Windows handles on the first attempt and the exception hid the report.

Two earlier attempts at this row on this platform are recorded here rather than discarded, because
what they found is worth keeping and neither was a defect in the product.

The first ran under an allowed-tools list that granted the control plane and the roles but not the
harness Workflow tool. /cycle:run is a dynamic workflow, so it could not start one - and it did not
fail either: the model did the work by hand instead, leaving a dirty tree, no workflow in the store
and sessions that cost pennies. From the outside that looked like a stalled delivery. It was a
missing permission, and the run script now grants Workflow and Skill explicitly, with the reason
written next to them.

The second, on the earlier bench, reached state `delivery` with 4 reviews, 2 arbitrations and 2
repair cycles - a genuinely contested cycle where the arbiter rejected, the executor produced a
scope violation and a plan defect, and a second arbitration approved - and then ran out of resume
sessions one short of the promotion. That is why the bench now spends three resumes rather than two:
a contested cycle needs more sessions than a straight-through one, and stopping a session early
reports a stalled delivery where there was only an exhausted budget.

Driven by tests-debug/recovery.mjs against the installed 1.0.23 artifact. A fresh git fixture, then
/cycle:run full started in a child process and polled until the control plane reported a registered
workflow. The session was then killed by process tree, hard, with no signal handling and no chance
to finish writing: a recovery that only survives a polite shutdown is not one. The kill landed at
state `architecture`.

What survived it: the plane still answered for the project, held the same workflow id and not a new
one, and carried the original request verbatim. The history chain was readable and recorded
workflow.started.

Reopening: a fresh session ran /cycle:resume, answered without error, and named the workflow that
was already there rather than starting another. Afterwards the plane still held that one workflow,
the request was still the user's own text, and the append-only record had only grown across the
kill - nothing was lost. It reattached at state `architecture`, which is where it was killed.

Fourteen assertions, all passed, 0.92 USD. The workflow was cancelled at the end deliberately: this
row is about reattaching, not about finishing, and a cycle left running would have cost more to
prove nothing extra.
